questions_and_answers.question_text: What is the literal meaning of duìbuqǐ?
In what situations is duìbuqǐ used?
In what situation is duìbuqǐ NOT used?
What is the order of sentence elements in Měiguo shū wǒmen bú mài?
What position does the object Měiguo shū occupy?
Is the bú mài at the end of this sentence a yes/no-choice question ending?

answers.answer_text: No — it is not, and the phrase keeps its tones in this sentence.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "I'm sorry, we don't sell American books here."

answers.answer_text: Duìbuqǐ, Měiguo shū wǒmen bú mài.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Which English speakers use this same word order?

answers.answer_text: Some speakers of English use the same topic-subject-verb order.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Which word would you NOT use to express sympathy at a relative's death?
Write the Chinese question meaning "Do you have any American books here?"

answers.answer_text: Nǐmen zhèli yǒu Měiguo shū meiyou?

articles.text:
8. A: Nǐmen zhèli yǒu Měiguo shū            Do you have any American books here?
      meiyou?
   B: Duìbuqǐ, Měiguo shū wǒmen             I'm sorry, we don't sell American
      bú mài.                               books here.

Notes on No. 8

Duìbuqǐ literally means "unable to face (you)." This word is used to say "I'm sorry" when you bump into a person, arrive late, and so on. It is not the word for "I'm sorry" when you sympathize with someone else's misfortune (e.g., when a relative dies).

Měiguo shū wǒmen bú mài: In this sentence, Měiguo shū, the object of the verb mài, occurs at the beginning, in topic position. Here the order of the sentence elements is topic, subject, verb. Some speakers of English use this same word order. Compare:

Měiguo shū  |  wǒmen  |  bú mài.
(American books  |  we  |  don't sell.)

Notice that bú mài is not the ending of a yes/no-choice question. The phrase keeps its tones in this sentence.
